items.title: Onaje Allan Gumbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001
items.q: being connected with another person who has been a mentor to me, Billy Taylor.

ctx.x: My name is Monk Rowe and we are filming in New York City for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive and I’m pleased to have my old friend, Onaje Allan Gumbs with me today, who is a marvelous piano player and arranger and composer, and manages to make a life in music in New York City, which I think is saying something.

Yes, yeah. That’s kind of a mouthful. It’s not the easiest thing to do. But one thing I learned early on, even as a teenager, was the ability to enjoy all genres of music. So jazz has always been my foundation. As a matter of fact my first real introduction to jazz was watching TV and looking at “Peter Gunn” and “Mr. Lucky,” which was scored by Henry Mancini. So needless to say Henry Mancini had an integral part in my development as a musician and a music lover. And I used to go to every film he scored. And…

realizing that I’d like to be a part of all this kind of music. So to shuttle between different styles of music was not a big thing for me, through high school I was playing with a Latin jazz band that was structured after Cal Tjader. The leader was a vibraphone player, the percussionist was Jerry Gonzalez of Fort Apache fame and his brother Andy Gonzalez. It was at the Music and Art High School in New York. And so I was at that band and at the same time I was working with one of my first mentors named Leroy…
